analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license to own handguns and certain semiautomatic rifles, with all sales recorded through licensed dealers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Tammy Duckworth on June 6, 2018, attracted no cosponsors and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required anyone who owns a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle that accepts a detachable magazine holding more than 10 rounds to obtain a federal firearm owner license — a photo ID card renewable every five years, with a fee capped at $10. Every sale or transfer of one of these guns would have to go through a licensed dealer who verifies the buyer's license and reports the sale to a new federal record-of-sale system, and background checks would extend to private transfers. It would also require reporting lost or stolen guns within 72 hours, add penalties for leaving guns accessible to children, and fund federal research on gun injuries.
analysis.who_benefits: People living with gun violence — the bill's stated goal is keeping guns away from prohibited buyers, making every transfer traceable, and requiring owners to know safe storage. The bill is named for Blair Holt, a Chicago high school student killed shielding a classmate on a bus in 2007.

how_it_helps.text: Anyone wanting to own a handgun or a covered semiautomatic rifle would need a federal license, issued after a check that screens for felony convictions, domestic-violence orders, recent violent misdemeanors, and mental-health commitments [S3].

All sales and transfers of covered guns would have to be processed through a licensed dealer who confirms the buyer's license is valid and records the transaction, and a federal record-of-sale system would be created for tracing guns used in crime [S3].

Background checks would extend to private transfers, which are currently exempt from federal checks, with narrow exceptions for close family and short-term loans between people who know each other [S3].
Owners would have to report lost or stolen guns within 72 hours, and adults could face up to 5 years in prison if a child accesses a stored loaded gun and someone is killed or seriously hurt [S3].
The Attorney General would have to run a firearm injury clearinghouse, study smart-gun technology, and publish annual findings — federal research on gun deaths that is currently constrained [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Current gun owners, who would have to apply for a license, keep their address current, and report lost or stolen guns on pain of criminal penalty; licensed dealers, who would handle and document every private transfer; and gun manufacturers, whose sales records would feed the federal system.

drawbacks.text: The bill deletes the existing legal ban on establishing a firearm registration system and directs the Attorney General to build a federal record of sale covering every licensed transfer [S3]. Gun-rights groups and many gun owners object to this as a de facto national gun registry.

Knowingly possessing a covered gun without a license would carry up to 10 years in prison, and a denied or revoked owner would have 48 hours to transfer any guns out of their control [S3] — a broad federal crime covering millions of firearms.

Every private transfer would require a trip to a licensed dealer, likely with a transfer fee and wait time, and the exceptions are narrow — for example, a 30-day loan only between people who personally know each other [S3].

Applicants must certify they were not a mental-health patient in the prior five years and authorize release of their mental-health records [S3], which critics argue could discourage people from seeking care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill takes the broadest approach available — universal licensing plus recorded transfers — which gives it strong tracing and screening power but also imposes real burdens on lawful owners and creates a federal database many will never accept. The fee cap ($10) and state-certification option soften the cost, but the 10-year penalty for unlicensed possession and the registry question mean even many gun-violence-reduction supporters prefer narrower bills. As written, it was the maximal version of gun regulation, and it had essentially no political support.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on June 6, 2018, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Duckworth introduced the Blair Holt Firearm Owner Licensing and Record of Sale Act on June 6, 2018, with Sen. Dick Durbin introducing it on her behalf [S1] [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill had zero cosponsors for its entire life [S4].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners and organizations opposed to federal licensing kept the status quo intact: no federal license requirement, no federal record-of-sale system, and no change to private transfer rules. The firearms industry also avoided the new recordkeeping and reporting obligations. Nobody who wanted stronger federal gun laws gained anything.

for.name: Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill; it was the only gun-licensing bill she introduced under this name in the 115th Congress.

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on Duckworth's behalf when it was read to the Senate.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral on June 6, 2018 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over firearms law
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill beyond referral for the remaining seven months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of any party, and it sat in the Republican-led Judiciary Committee until Congress ended.

industries.note: Every private sale or transfer of a covered gun would have to run through a licensed dealer, who verifies the buyer's license and files the paperwork — creating a guaranteed stream of paid transfer transactions. The cost of that mandated middleman falls on ordinary buyers and sellers.

Dealers would report manufacturer, model, and serial number of every covered transfer to a federal record-of-sale system, adding compliance exposure, and a licensing requirement could shrink the pool of legal buyers. But any gun sales that do occur would flow through the mandated dealer channel.

Millions of current handgun and semiautomatic rifle owners would need a federal license, face criminal penalties for lapses in reporting, and have their transfers recorded. The bill's premise is that these burdens buy public safety; many owners see only the burden.
